```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# The ragg device writes smaller figure files; without it the default is used.
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(bayesEfron.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
has_loo <- requireNamespace("loo", quietly = TRUE)
has_bayesplot <- requireNamespace("bayesplot", quietly = TRUE)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
big <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
```

This vignette explains how to check a fit before you use its results. We
start with `diagnose()`, which reports in a few lines on whether the
sampler did its work and whether the results depend on where the grid
ends. We then check whether the fitted model describes the estimates it
was given. That takes a plot and some judgment. The last section covers
what to do about a warning.

```{r library}
library(bayesEfron)
```

The reason to check first is that every number a fit reports is computed
from the draws of a Markov chain. The numbers describe the posterior
distribution only if the chains have reached that distribution and have
moved through it often enough. You cannot tell from the results whether
they have, because a fit that has not converged prints a table of
estimates that looks like any other. The diagnostics are the evidence on
that point, so read them before the estimates.

## Running `diagnose()`

We use `krw_fit` as the main example. It is a fit that comes with the
package: the model for the callback gaps at 97 firms from
`vignette("bayesEfron")`, fitted with the default grid and the default
sampler settings. We pass it to `diagnose()`.

```{r diagnose}
fit <- krw_fit
diag <- diagnose(fit)
diag
```

`diagnose()` does not run the sampler again. It collects what
`bayes_efron_fit()` computed when the model was fitted. Each printed line
gives the worst value of a diagnostic, with the quantity or the site that
it belongs to in parentheses, or a total count for the divergent
transitions and the iterations at the maximum tree depth. The six lines
from `Rhat max` to
`E-BFMI min` are the sampler diagnostics, and the lines under `Grid` are
the grid diagnostics, where "end" means the lower or the upper limit of
the grid. The remaining lines (`Model family`, `Runtime` and
`Effective params`) repeat information from the fit.

To see the outcome of each check, convert the result to a data frame,
which has one row for each check with its threshold and its status.

```{r checks}
as.data.frame(diag)[, c("diagnostic", "threshold", "rule", "status")]
```

The `rule` column gives the direction of the comparison: R-hat, for
example, should be at most 1.01. Every check has the status `"ok"`.

The result is a list, and three of its elements name the diagnostics that
need attention:

- `sampler_diagnostics_failed`, those that fail a check
- `sampler_diagnostics_warned`, those that get a warning
- `diagnostic_skipped`, those that could not be computed or were not
  compared with their thresholds

All three are empty here.

```{r flags}
lengths(diag[c("sampler_diagnostics_failed", "sampler_diagnostics_warned",
               "diagnostic_skipped")])
```

You will learn about a failed check even if you never call `diagnose()`,
because `bayes_efron_fit()` also issues a warning about it when it
returns.

## The six sampler diagnostics

The model is fitted with the No-U-Turn sampler (NUTS) of @hoffman2014.
This sampler moves through the posterior distribution in a sequence of
small steps, with a step size that it sets during warmup, and each
iteration is a path of many steps. R-hat and the two effective sample
sizes describe the draws that result. The other three diagnostics
describe the paths.

R-hat compares the chains with one another. If they have all settled on
the same distribution, the variation between chains is no larger than the
variation within them, and R-hat is close to 1. The effective sample size
(ESS) is the number of independent draws that the correlated draws of the
chains are worth. The bulk ESS concerns the center of the distribution,
and with it the posterior means, whereas the tail ESS concerns the 5% and
95% quantiles, and with them the intervals. @vehtari2021 recommend that
the draws be used only if, for every quantity, R-hat is below 1.01 and
both effective sample sizes are at least 400 when 4 chains are run.
`diagnose()` lists a warning when a value falls short of these
recommendations, and it counts an R-hat above 1.05 as a failed check.

A divergent transition, or divergence, means that the sampler met a
region of the posterior distribution that it could not follow with the
step size it had chosen. The draws may then miss part of the
distribution, so even one divergent transition is a failed check. An
iteration reaches the maximum tree depth when its path is cut short at
the greatest length that `max_treedepth` allows. That makes the sampler
less efficient, which shows in the effective sample sizes, but it does
not bias the draws, so it is listed as a warning. The energy Bayesian
fraction of missing information (E-BFMI) is computed for each chain and
is low when the chain moves slowly between the high and the low levels of
the log density. A warning is listed below 0.3, the value below which
cmdstanr prints a message of its own.

```{r quantities, include = FALSE}
blocks <- table(sub("[[].*", "", names(diag$rhat)))
stopifnot(length(diag$rhat) == 114L, blocks[["alpha"]] == 6L,
          blocks[["log_g"]] == 101L, blocks[["lambda"]] == 1L,
          blocks[["lp__"]] == 1L, sum(blocks) - 109L == 5L,
          all(c("mean_g", "sd_g") %in% names(blocks)),
          !any(grepl("^theta", names(diag$rhat))),
          isFALSE(attr(fit$metadata, "storage")$site_draws))
```

R-hat and the effective sample sizes are computed for every quantity in
the draws. For these data a default fit stores `r length(diag$rhat)`
quantities:

- the log density `lp__`
- the `r blocks[["alpha"]]` spline coefficients `alpha`
- the parameter `lambda`, which sets how strongly those coefficients are
  held toward zero
- the logarithm of $g$ at each of the `r blocks[["log_g"]]` grid points,
  `log_g`
- five quantities computed from those, among them the mean and the
  standard deviation of $g$

Here we print R-hat and the effective sample sizes for six of them.

```{r by-quantity}
shown <- c("lambda", "mean_g", "sd_g", "log_g[1]", "log_g[51]", "log_g[101]")
data.frame(rhat = round(diag$rhat[shown], 3),
           ess_bulk = round(diag$ess_bulk[shown]),
           ess_tail = round(diag$ess_tail[shown]))
```

A site's effect is not among the stored quantities. What a default fit
reports about a site is computed from the draws of $g$, so the checks of
`log_g` at the grid points are the ones that matter for the sites. A fit
made with `site_draws = TRUE` also stores draws for each site, and they
are checked with the rest.

```{r worst, include = FALSE}
stored <- list(krw_fit, raudenbush_fit, twin_towers_fit)
stopifnot(
  max(diag$rhat) < 1.01, min(diag$ess_bulk) > 400, min(diag$ess_tail) > 400,
  sum(diag$divergences) == 0, sum(diag$max_treedepth) == 0,
  min(diag$ebfmi) > 0.3,
  # Neither a missing nor an infinite value in the stored fits.
  all(vapply(stored, function(x) all(is.finite(diagnose(x)$rhat)), logical(1))),
  all(vapply(stored, function(x) length(diagnose(x)$diagnostic_skipped) == 0L,
             logical(1)))
)
print(c(max(diag$rhat), min(diag$ess_bulk), min(diag$ess_tail), min(diag$ebfmi)))
```

For the firms the largest R-hat is `r num(max(diag$rhat), 3)`, the
smallest bulk and tail effective sample sizes are
`r big(min(diag$ess_bulk))` and `r big(min(diag$ess_tail))`, there are no
divergent transitions, no iteration reaches the maximum tree depth, and
the smallest E-BFMI is `r num(min(diag$ebfmi))`. All six diagnostics
pass.

R-hat can also be `NA` or infinite. It is `NA` for a quantity that has
the same value in every draw, which is not a sign of trouble. A quantity
that stays at one value within each chain, but at different values in
different chains, has an infinite R-hat, and `diagnose()` counts that as
a failed check because the chains have not mixed at all. See `?diagnose`
for the details. If the whole run has fewer than 400 draws, R-hat and the
effective sample sizes are returned but not compared with their
thresholds, and `diagnostic_skipped` names the checks that were left out.

## Plotting the sampler diagnostics

`plot_diagnostics()` shows R-hat and the effective sample sizes of all
the quantities at once, so you can tell whether a poor value is one of a
kind or one of many. We select the panels for the sampler with `what`.

```{r diagnostics-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Three panels for the callback fit: R-hat, bulk and tail effective sample sizes of the monitored quantities in blocks, all on the good side of the dashed threshold lines."}
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = c("rhat", "ess"))
```

```{r plot-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(names(which.min(diag$ess_bulk)) == "lp__",
          grepl("^log_g", names(which.min(diag$ess_tail))),
          diag$ess_bulk[["mean_g"]] > 12000,
          sum(grepl("^log_g", names(diag$rhat))) > 30)
```

The quantities are grouped in blocks. A block of up to 30 quantities is
shown as points. A larger block, here the `r blocks[["log_g"]]` values of
`log_g`, is shown as a box with its worst value as a point. The name
beside a block is the name of its worst quantity. Dashed lines mark the
thresholds 1.01 and 400, and a dotted line marks 1.05. The caption gives
the other three diagnostics: divergent transitions, iterations at the
maximum tree depth, and the smallest E-BFMI.

In this fit every point is on the good side of its dashed line. The
smallest bulk ESS belongs to the log density and the smallest tail ESS to
a value of `log_g`. The mean of $g$ has a bulk ESS of
`r big(diag$ess_bulk[["mean_g"]])` from 12,000 draws. An ESS above the
number of draws is possible when successive draws are negatively
correlated.

## Grid diagnostics

With point masses at the grid points (`component = "point"`, the
default), no effect can lie beyond the ends of the grid. A range that is
too narrow therefore distorts the results for the sites near its ends,
however well the chains have mixed. Two values in the `grid` element of
the result bear on this. The first is in `diag$grid$ends`, a data frame
with one row for each end.

```{r grid-ends}
diag$grid$ends[, c("end", "value", "set_by", "mass", "label", "status")]
```

For each end, `mass` is the largest proportion of posterior probability
that any site has in the outer 2% of the range, and `label` is that site.
If a site has more than 5% of its posterior probability there, its result
depends on where the grid ends. For the firms the larger of the two
values is `r num(100 * max(diag$grid$ends$mass), 2)`%.

The second value is the standard deviation of $g$: `sd_g` describes its
posterior distribution, and `sd_g_prior` the distribution that the prior
alone would give it on the same grid.

```{r grid-sd}
round(diag$grid$sd_g, 4)
round(diag$grid$sd_g_prior, 4)
```

```{r grid-facts, include = FALSE}
towers <- diagnose(twin_towers_fit)$grid$ends
lower <- towers[towers$end == "lower", ]
stopifnot(
  all(diag$grid$ends$status == "ok"), max(diag$grid$ends$mass) < 0.05,
  diag$grid$share == 0.02, diag$grid$threshold == 0.05,
  diag$grid$sd_g[["q95"]] < diag$grid$sd_g_prior[["q5"]],
  all(towers$set_by == "pilot"), lower$status == "note", lower$mass > 0.05,
  lower$label == "774", lower$estimate_beyond > 1,
  length(diagnose(twin_towers_fit)$sampler_diagnostics_warned) == 0L
)
print(lower)
```

The posterior mean is `r num(diag$grid$sd_g[["mean"]], 3)` and the prior
median is `r num(diag$grid$sd_g_prior[["q50"]], 3)`, so the data have
moved the spread of $g$ well away from what the grid alone implies. When
the two are close, the data have done little to determine the tails of
$g$, and it is worth comparing fits on other ranges.

`plot_diagnostics()` shows both values when `what` includes `"grid"`.
This time we plot them for `twin_towers_fit`, the fit of the 1,500
simulated sites from `vignette("twin-towers")`.

```{r grid-plot, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Two panels for the fit of the simulated sites. Left: the largest posterior mass of a site in the outer part of the range, near zero at the upper end and, at the lower end, well beyond the dashed line at 0.05. Right: the 90 percent interval of the standard deviation of the distribution of effects under the prior, wide, and under the posterior, narrow and lower."}
plot_diagnostics(twin_towers_fit, what = "grid")
```

The mass at the lower end is well beyond the dashed line, so we print the
ends for this fit.

```{r grid-ends-towers}
diagnose(twin_towers_fit)$grid$ends[, c("end", "set_by", "mass", "label",
                                        "estimate_beyond", "status")]
```

At the lower end a site has `r num(100 * lower$mass, 1)`% of its
posterior probability in the outer part of the range, and yet
`diagnose()` reports no warning: the status is `"note"`. The default
method moved this end in (`set_by` is `"pilot"`). It moves an end only as
far as the point where the pilot fit, a short preliminary fit on a wider
range, put the end of $g$. A site with an estimate beyond such an
end is shrunk to it. The estimate of site `r lower$label` lies
`r num(lower$estimate_beyond, 1)` standard errors beyond the lower end,
and the mass is reported as a note. At an end that was given in
`support`, or that follows from the estimates alone, the same mass leads
to a warning that names the site. See `vignette("choosing-a-grid")` for
what to do in each case.

The last line under `Grid` gives the part of the grid spanned by the
central 99.9% of the estimate of $g$. It is informative only when there
are many sites. Like the summaries of a fit, all the grid
diagnostics are computed from the draws stored in the fit.

## A posterior predictive check

A model can pass all the checks so far and still be a poor description of
the data, because convergence only means that the draws describe the
model's posterior distribution. `plot_ppc()` is a posterior predictive
check: it compares the estimates with what the fitted model predicts for
them.

Under the model, the distribution of an estimate is the distribution of
effects convolved with a normal distribution whose standard deviation is
the site's standard error. We compare
each estimate with that distribution through its probability integral
transform (PIT), the probability that the fitted model gives to a smaller
estimate at that site. If $g$ were known and the model described the
estimates, the PIT values would be spread evenly between 0 and 1. The
check compares the PIT values of the fitted model with the uniform
distribution.

```{r ppc, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "The empirical distribution function of the probability integral transforms of the 97 estimates less the uniform one, a stepped line that stays inside a gray band."}
plot_ppc(fit)
```

```{r ppc-facts, include = FALSE}
# The points at which the line of a plot_ppc() result lies outside its band.
outside_band <- function(plot) {
  band <- ggplot2::layer_data(plot, 1L)
  line <- ggplot2::layer_data(plot, 3L)
  stopifnot(nrow(band) == nrow(line), isTRUE(all.equal(band$x, line$x)))
  excess <- pmax(band$ymin - line$y, line$y - band$ymax)
  data.frame(x = line$x, excess = excess)[excess > 1e-8, ]
}
stopifnot(nrow(outside_band(plot_ppc(fit))) == 0L,
          nrow(ggplot2::layer_data(plot_ppc(fit), 3L)) == 201L)
if (has_loo) {
  left_out <- outside_band(plot_ppc(fit, loo = TRUE))
  # One point of 201, near 0.9, by one estimate in 97.
  stopifnot(nrow(left_out) == 1L, abs(left_out$x - 0.9) < 0.02,
            abs(left_out$excess - 1 / 97) < 1e-6)
  pareto_k <- loo::loo(fit)$diagnostics$pareto_k
  stopifnot(length(pareto_k) == 97L, max(pareto_k) < 0.5)
  print(left_out); print(max(pareto_k))
}
```

The line is the empirical distribution function of the 97 PIT values
minus the distribution function of the uniform distribution. The band is
where that difference would lie with probability 95% at each point if the
values were independent draws from the uniform distribution, as they
would be with $g$ known. However, the PIT values of a fitted model all
depend on the same estimate of $g$, and the band makes no allowance for
that. It is a reference, and 95% is not the probability that the line of
a fitted model lies inside it at a given point. The line for the firms
stays inside the band.

The model was fitted to the same estimates that it is checked against,
which makes the check lenient. With `loo = TRUE`, the PIT of each site is
computed from the posterior distribution without that site (the LOO-PIT),
by Pareto smoothed importance sampling [@vehtari2017]. This needs the loo
package.

```{r ppc-loo, eval = has_loo, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "The same plot with each probability integral transform computed without its own site. The stepped line dips just below the gray band at one point near 0.9."}
plot_ppc(fit, loo = TRUE)
```

The line now drops below the band at one of the 201 points at which it is
plotted, near 0.9, by the weight of a single estimate, 1/97. Leaving out a
site's estimate keeps it from being used in its own check, but any two of
the PIT values still rest on nearly the same estimates, so they are not
independent. The band remains a pointwise reference, and a departure at one
of many plotted points is weak evidence against the model. A departure
over a long stretch would be a reason to examine the likelihood, the
standard errors and the grid more closely.

The importance sampling has a diagnostic of its own, the Pareto k of each
site. `plot_loo()` plots the Pareto k values against the threshold above
which the result for a site should not be trusted. A site above the
threshold would change the posterior distribution substantially if it
were removed. No firm is near it: the largest Pareto k of the 97 is below
0.5.

A check like this can detect that the estimates are not what a normal
likelihood with the given standard errors and some $g$ on this grid would
produce. The cause may be standard errors that are too small, a grid that
is too narrow, or too few spline functions. Passing the check is not
evidence that the shape of $g$ is right. Distributions of effects that
differ in shape give nearly the same distribution of noisy estimates, so
a model can pass with a wrong $g$.

## Thinned fits

When `thin` is set, `bayes_efron_fit()` stores only part of the draws.
The example fits in the package were made with `thin = 15`, which stores
1 iteration in 15, or 800 of the 12,000 draws, so that the package stays
small. The sampler diagnostics in `diagnose()` and `plot_diagnostics()`
are still computed from the whole run, because it is the whole run that
shows whether the chains converged. The summaries of the fit and the grid
diagnostics are computed from the stored draws. How precise they are is a
separate question, which we can answer from the stored draws themselves
with the posterior package. We do this for three quantities.

```{r kept}
kept <- posterior::subset_draws(fit$draws,
                                variable = c("lambda", "mean_g", "sd_g"))
posterior::summarize_draws(kept, "mean", "sd", "mcse_mean", "ess_bulk")
```

```{r kept-facts, include = FALSE}
kept_sd_g <- posterior::summarize_draws(
  posterior::subset_draws(fit$draws, variable = "sd_g"),
  "sd", "mcse_mean", "ess_bulk"
)
storage <- attr(fit$metadata, "storage")
stopifnot(storage$thin == 15L, storage$iterations * storage$chains == 800L,
          posterior::ndraws(fit$draws) == 800L,
          kept_sd_g$ess_bulk > 600, kept_sd_g$ess_bulk < 800,
          diag$ess_bulk[["sd_g"]] > 5000,
          kept_sd_g$mcse_mean / kept_sd_g$sd < 0.05)
print(kept_sd_g)
```

The draws that thinning discards were correlated with their neighbors, so
the 800 that remain are nearly independent. For the standard deviation of
$g$ they have a bulk ESS of `r big(kept_sd_g$ess_bulk)`, compared with
`r big(diag$ess_bulk[["sd_g"]])` for the 12,000 draws of the whole run,
and the Monte Carlo standard error of its posterior mean is
`r num(100 * kept_sd_g$mcse_mean / kept_sd_g$sd, 1)`% of the posterior
standard deviation. A fit of your own stores every draw unless you set
`thin`, and then the sampler diagnostics and the summaries describe the
same draws.

## Looking at the chains

When a diagnostic is poor, plots of the chains can show where the problem
is. `plot_mcmc()` makes several bayesplot plots directly from a fit. We
start with a trace plot, in which each chain is a line over the
iterations. Chains that have converged cover the same range, and none of
them drifts.

```{r trace, eval = has_bayesplot, fig.height = 2.6, fig.alt = "Trace plots of lambda and of the standard deviation of the distribution of effects for the callback fit: four chains of 200 kept draws each, overlapping."}
plot_mcmc(fit, type = "trace", pars = c("lambda", "sd_g"))
```

Each line has 200 points, the stored draws of one chain.

The plot that goes with E-BFMI is the bayesplot energy plot, which
compares the spread of the energy over the iterations with the size of
its changes from one iteration to the next. It needs neighboring
iterations, so `plot_mcmc()` throws an error for a thinned fit such as
the example fits. Among them, the fit of the 19 studies has the lowest
E-BFMI, `r num(min(diagnose(raudenbush_fit)$ebfmi))`, just above the
threshold, so these are the data to look at. The code below fits them
without thinning and plots the energy. It is shown but not run here,
because it calls the sampler.

```{r energy, eval = FALSE}
studies <- bayes_efron_fit(raudenbush1985, seed = 1985)
plot_mcmc(studies, type = "energy")
```

```{r chains-facts, include = FALSE}
ebfmi <- vapply(stored, function(x) min(diagnose(x)$ebfmi), numeric(1))
stopifnot(which.min(ebfmi) == 2L, ebfmi[2] > 0.3, ebfmi[2] < 0.35)
if (has_bayesplot) {
  stopifnot(inherits(tryCatch(plot_mcmc(fit, type = "energy"),
                              error = function(e) e), "bef_invalid_args"),
            max(bayesplot::neff_ratio(fit)) < 1.5)
}
```

For other bayesplot plots, a fit has methods for `nuts_params()`,
`log_posterior()`, `rhat()` and `neff_ratio()`, which return what the
plot functions take as input. The last two return the values of the whole
run. For example:

```{r bayesplot, eval = FALSE}
bayesplot::mcmc_rhat(bayesplot::rhat(fit))
bayesplot::mcmc_neff(bayesplot::neff_ratio(fit))
bayesplot::mcmc_nuts_divergence(bayesplot::nuts_params(fit),
                                bayesplot::log_posterior(fit))
```

## Responding to a warning

The remedies for the sampler are arguments of `bayes_efron_fit()`. The
calls below show three of them.

```{r remedies, eval = FALSE}
dat <- as_bef_data(krw_discrimination, site = "firm_name")

# Divergent transitions: smaller steps.
bayes_efron_fit(dat, adapt_delta = 0.99)

# Iterations that reach the maximum tree depth: allow longer paths.
bayes_efron_fit(dat, max_treedepth = 12)

# Small effective sample sizes, or R-hat between 1.01 and 1.05: run longer.
bayes_efron_fit(dat, iter_warmup = 2000, iter_sampling = 6000)
```

Before you change the sampler settings, though, ask whether the grid is
the cause. Two sets of results in the package suggest why.

First, the range can be too narrow. `vignette("choosing-a-grid")`
compares three ranges for the 19 studies of `raudenbush1985`, fitted with
the same seed and the same sampler settings. We print that comparison
with the narrowest range first.

```{r narrow}
ranges <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "raudenbush_ranges.rds",
                              package = "bayesEfron"))
ranges <- as.data.frame(ranges)[order(ranges$expansion), ]
ranges[, c("expansion", "lower", "upper", "divergences", "max_rhat",
           "end_mass")]
```

```{r narrow-facts, include = FALSE}
narrow <- ranges[1, ]
stopifnot(nrow(ranges) == 3L, narrow$expansion == min(ranges$expansion),
          narrow$divergences > 0, all(ranges$divergences[2:3] == 0),
          narrow$end_mass > 0.05, all(ranges$end_mass[2:3] < 0.05),
          narrow$max_rhat > 1.01, all(ranges$max_rhat[2:3] < 1.01))
```

On the narrowest range the run has `r narrow$divergences` divergent
transitions, an R-hat above 1.01, and a study with
`r num(100 * narrow$end_mass, 1)`% of its posterior probability in the
outer 2% of the range (`end_mass`). On the two wider ranges there are no
divergent transitions. We have not checked whether a smaller step size (a
higher `adapt_delta`) would also remove them on the narrowest range. But
the mass at the end of the grid points to a cause that no sampler setting
changes: the range stops where the data still put an effect. The remedy
is a wider range.

Second, the range can be wider than the data need.
`vignette("twin-towers")` fits the same 1,500 simulated sites on several
grids, and we print three of those fits.

```{r wide}
towers <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "twin_towers_comparison.rds",
                              package = "bayesEfron"))$table[c(5, 2, 1), ]
data.frame(lower = round(towers$lower, 1), upper = round(towers$upper, 1),
           M = towers$M, at_max_treedepth = towers$treedepth_hits,
           min_ess_bulk = round(towers$min_ess_bulk),
           seconds = round(towers$sampling_seconds))
```

```{r wide-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(
  towers$rule[1] == "paper_realdata", towers$rule[2:3] == "pilot",
  towers$w1[1] > towers$w1[2], towers$w1[2] > towers$w1[3],
  towers$M == c(6, 6, 8), towers$treedepth_hits[1] > 5000,
  towers$treedepth_hits[2] > 0, towers$treedepth_hits[3] == 0,
  towers$treedepth_share[1] > 0.4, towers$treedepth_share[2] < 0.02,
  diff(towers$sampling_seconds) < 0, towers$divergences == 0,
  towers$max_rhat < 1.01, abs(diff(range(towers$coverage_90))) < 0.01,
  (towers$upper[1] - towers$lower[1]) / (towers$upper[2] - towers$lower[2]) > 3
)
```

The first row is the wide range that follows from the estimates alone
(`grid_method = "paper_realdata"`), which is more than 3 times as wide as
the range that the default method chooses. On the wide range
`r num(100 * towers$treedepth_share[1], 0)`% of the iterations reach the
maximum tree depth, and sampling takes
`r round(towers$sampling_seconds[1])` seconds. On the default range, in
the second row, the proportion is
`r num(100 * towers$treedepth_share[2], 1)`% and the time is
`r round(towers$sampling_seconds[2])` seconds. In the third row, with 8
spline functions instead of 6, no iteration reaches the maximum tree
depth. All three runs pass the R-hat check, so in this data set the wide
range costs time and, as `vignette("twin-towers")` shows, a less accurate
estimate of $g$, but not convergence.

```{r panels-facts, include = FALSE}
panels <- read.csv(system.file("verification", "panels-convergence.csv",
                               package = "bayesEfron"), check.names = FALSE)
defaults <- panels[panels$setting == "defaults", ]
eight <- panels[panels$setting == "M = 8", ]
old <- panels[grepl("0.3.0", panels$setting, fixed = TRUE), ]
stopifnot(nrow(defaults) == 1L, nrow(eight) == 1L, nrow(old) == 1L,
          panels$panels == 20, defaults[["rhat_above_1.01"]] == 0,
          old[["rhat_above_1.01"]] > 10, old[["rhat_above_1.05"]] > 0,
          old$treedepth_share_median > 0.5,
          round(defaults$inclusion, 3) == round(old$inclusion, 3),
          abs(defaults$inclusion - 0.9) < 0.005,
          (0.9 - eight$inclusion) / eight$inclusion_se > 2,
          (0.9 - eight$inclusion) / eight$inclusion_se < 3)
```

Across simulated data sets, a wide range can also cost convergence.
`vignette("implementation")` tabulates fits of `r defaults$panels`
simulated data sets of 1,500 sites. With the defaults, none of the fits
has an R-hat above 1.01. With the settings of version 0.3.0 of the
package (`settings = "0.3.0"`), which use the wide range and that
version's Stan program, `r old[["rhat_above_1.01"]]` of the
`r defaults$panels` fits have an R-hat above 1.01, and
`r old[["rhat_above_1.05"]]` have one above 1.05. Both the range and the
Stan program differ from the defaults, so this comparison cannot tell us
which of the two is responsible.

The same fits show what the diagnostics measure. The coverage of the 90%
intervals (the proportion of the true effects inside them) is
`r num(defaults$inclusion, 3)` under both settings. So the diagnostics do
not measure how wrong a fit is. They tell us whether there is evidence
that the chains have sampled the posterior distribution, and for most of
the fits made with `settings = "0.3.0"` that evidence is missing. Ease of
sampling is also not a reason to prefer a specification: with 8 spline
functions the coverage is `r num(eight$inclusion, 3)`, more than 2
standard errors below 0.90.

These results come from two data sets and one simulation design. That is
too little for a rule, but it suggests which questions to ask first:

- If there is a warning about an end of the grid, widen the range before
  anything else.
- If many iterations reach the maximum tree depth, or the effective
  sample sizes are small, first check whether the range is far wider than
  the estimates need. If it is not, increase `max_treedepth` or run
  longer.
- A fit with more spline functions may sample more easily. If you switch
  to one, compare the results of the two fits as well as their
  diagnostics.
- If there are divergent transitions and no warning about the grid, raise
  `adapt_delta`. See `vignette("teacher-expectancy")` for what that did
  for data sets of 19 studies.
- If an R-hat is above 1.05, do not use the draws.
